chunks.content: Key Points Introduction Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a hemodynamic condition defined, according to the 6th world Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) as mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) above 20 mmHg at rest [ , ]. PH is a progressive disease, causing severe symptoms with a poor prognosis leading to right sided heart failure (RHF) in group 2 PH, which is the majority of patients with PH undergoing mitral valve repair surgery. The prevalence of PH in general is agreed to be higher in young patients, particularly females. However, the prevalence among patients above 65 years is also likely to occur owing to other underlying comorbidities, such as left heart disease. On the other hand, USA and Europe data supports the high prevalence among the elderly even in case of arterial PH [ , ]. PH can be primary or secondary. Secondary causes of PH include, but not limited to, underlying pathology (such as pulmonary and left sided cardiac disease), drugs, toxins, or certain infections [ , ]. Clinically, PH can be classified into five groups based on the pathophysiology: group 1, caused by pulmonary artery disease, which could be idiopathic or hereditary; group 2, caused by left sided heart disease e.g., left sided heart failure; group 3, caused by pulmonary disease and/or hypoxia; group 4, caused by pulmonary artery obstruction e.g., chronic thromboembolism; and finally group 5, which can be caused by multifactorial mechanisms. Group 2 and 3 PH are frequently found in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. In patients with group 1 PH, hemodynamics are characterized by an elevated mPAP above 20 mmHg, with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) ≤ 15 mmHg, reflecting isolated pulmonary vascular pathology. Conversely, in group 2 PH, which is linked to left heart disease including mitral valve disease, patients demonstrate both elevated mPAP and PCWP > 15 mmHg, indicative of pulmonary venous hypertension resulting from left-sided heart dysfunction. In mixed pre- and post-capillary PH, seen in some patients with advanced heart disease, both mPAP and PCWP are elevated, often accompanied by increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), highlighting the complex interplay between pulmonary vascular and left-sided heart dysfunction [ – ]. Regardless of the etiology, patients with PH express the same pathologic changes, including prolonged vasoconstriction and pulmonary vascular remodeling, which eventually lead to increased pulmonary vascular resistance, subsequently elevating the right ventricular pressure [ , ]. Pre-existing PH prior to cardiac surgery poses a significantly increased risk of morbidity and mortality which can be aggravated by multiple factors, including extracorporeal circulation, mechanical ventilation, and the use of general anesthesia [ – ]. Multiple mechanisms are attributed to right ventricular (RV) failure including: the elevated afterload resulting from the maladaptation to the increased vascular resistance, the poor contractile reserve of the right ventricle, and the arrest during the surgical procedure [ ]. Therefore, optimization of the perioperative cardiopulmonary pressures is paramount to avoid unnecessary adverse events such as acute right-sided heart failure and delayed extubating. Currently, available medical therapies for group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension target mostly one of three essential pathways: prostacyclin, endothelin (ET), and nitric oxide (NO) causing smooth muscle relaxation and pulmonary vasodilation with subsequent reduction in the pulmonary artery pressure [ ]. However, they are harmful in some cases of pulmonary venous hypertension as they can provoke pulmonary edema if in a patient with mitral valve disease [ ]. Thus, careful perioperative optimization of PH in patients undergoing cardiac surgery can be challenging with lack of existing knowledge in this area. The aim of this network meta-analysis is to compare the efficacy of various pulmonary vasodilators in perioperative optimization of PH in those patients with the goal of addressing the existing knowledge gap. Methods This network meta-analysis was carried out on the basis of a predetermined protocol registered in Open Science Framework with registration link https://doi.org/ 10.17605/OSF.IO/7HMJ2, and was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension statement for network meta-analysis (NMA PRISMA 2020) [ , ]. Search Strategy and Data Collection We conducted a comprehensive and systematic literature search of five electronic databases, including PubMed, Cochrane Central Registry of Controlled Trials, Scopus, Embase and Web of Science (WOS) from inception to 17 September 2024. The search strategy has been formulated based on the key terms of previous studies. These keywords were the interventions, the condition of interest and the type of surgery. The search Strategy was: (“mitral valve surgery” OR “valve surgery”) AND “Pulmonary hypertension” AND (“sildenafil” OR “levosimendan” OR “milrinone” OR “nitroglycerin” OR “dexmedetomidine” OR “iloprost” OR “nitric oxide” OR “dobutamine” OR “Sodium nitroprusside” OR “Prostacycline” OR “Enoximone”). We included only randomized-controlled trials (RCTs) involving vasodilator intervention and its impact on hemodynamics of pulmonary hypertension patients undergoing mitral valve surgery compared with another vasodilator or placebo group. The search Strategy was: (“mitral valve surgery” OR “valve surgery”) AND “Pulmonary hypertension” AND (“sildenafil” OR “levosimendan” OR “milrinone” OR “nitroglycerin” OR “dexmedetomidine” OR “iloprost” OR “nitric oxide” OR “dobutamine” OR “Sodium nitroprusside” OR “Prostacycline” OR “Enoximone”). We included only randomized-controlled trials (RCTs) involving vasodilator intervention and its impact on hemodynamics of pulmonary hypertension patients undergoing mitral valve surgery compared with another vasodilator or placebo group. We also searched the reference lists of the relevant RCTs to add any missing RCT from our preliminary search and clinicaltrials.gov to look for unpublished or ongoing studies. All RCTs were included with no language or publication period limitations. Selection Criteria We included studies that met the following requirements: (1) population: this review considered all studies that involved patients of any age and sex undergoing mitral valve surgery, and had pulmonary hypertension diagnosed using the gold standard right heart catheterization method or echocardiography. The cutoff values of diagnosing PH in the included studies were MPAP ≥ 25 mmHg or SPAP ≥ 35 mmHg. Studies that included combined interventions in one arm compared with placebo or control group in the other arm were excluded. (2) Interventions: studies where the experimental (or exposed) group received sildenafil, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, dexmedetomidine, iloprost, nitric oxide, or dobutamine treatment; (3) comparators: studies where the control group received sildenafil, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, dexmedetomidine, iloprost, nitric oxide, dobutamine, or placebo (patients who were not exposed to vasodilators therapy prior to or during the valve surgery); (4) outcomes: comparing the efficacy of different vasodilators in managing perioperative pulmonary hypertension. The efficacy was determined on the basis of the hemodynamic changes from perioperative period to the last available follow-up period in each study. The hemodynamic variables include heart rate (HR), mean arterial pressure (MAP), mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (C.I), central venous pressure (CVP), systolic pulmonary artery pressure (SPAP), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). All outcomes were continuous and expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and number of patients. (5) Study design: we included only randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Study Screening and Data Extraction Four reviewers independently screened the articles’ titles and abstracts based on the eligibility criteria of inclusion. Reviewers were blinded by each other's decisions. After exclusion of non-eligible studies, the remaining studies underwent full text screening by the same method. Conflicts were resolved through reviewers’ discussion with the assistance of the first review author to determine the final decision. The screening process was done using Rayyan software [ ]. We extracted the relevant data into three electronic sheets: (1) summary sheet: contains the basic information of each study, which are study design, country, number of centers, total participants, follow-up duration, main inclusion criteria, primary outcomes, and conclusion; (2) baseline sheet: contains the baseline characteristics of patients in each study. Baseline characteristics include age, sex, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and body mass index (BMI). The categorical data were shown as event frequency and its percentage whereas the continuous data were shown as mean and standard deviation. We extracted the mean and SD for the intervention group and the comparative group separately. For studies not measuring BMI and containing weight and height, we calculated BMI utilizing this equation: BMI (kg/m 2 ) = weight (Kg)/ height (m 2 ). (3) outcome sheet: this sheet is for the hemodynamics changes. Our outcomes of interest were heart rate (HR), mean arterial pressure (MAP), mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (C.I), central venous pressure (CVP), systolic pulmonary artery pressure (SPAP), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). We extracted outcome values at baseline and at the end of follow- up. All outcomes were expressed as mean ± SD. Not all studies contain all the prespecified outcomes, we considered these missing data in data cleaning and manipulation. For studies that report data in graphical format only, we used Web plot digitizer version to extract these data. Quality Assessment We used the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (ROB 2.0) [ ] to assess the quality of the eligible RCTs. It includes five domains of bias: randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Five reviewers independently reviewed the included studies. Studies were classified based on each domain separately into low risk, some concerns or high risk. Each domain’s final decision was taken based on significant questions answered with “yes,” “probably yes,” “probably no,” “no,” or “no information” according to algorithms suggested by ROB 2.0. Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (ROB 2.0) [ ] to assess the quality of the eligible RCTs. It includes five domains of bias: randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Five reviewers independently reviewed the included studies. Studies were classified based on each domain separately into low risk, some concerns or high risk. Each domain’s final decision was taken based on significant questions answered with “yes,” “probably yes,” “probably no,” “no,” or “no information” according to algorithms suggested by ROB 2.0. Any disagreements were resolved by discussion or with the assistance of the first review author. Statistical Analysis To carry out this network meta-analysis (NMA), we utilized the netmeta package accessible through RStudio. The data was aggregated as mean difference (MD) for continuous outcomes and risk ratio (RR) for dichotomous outcomes, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) provided for each outcome. We assessed and measured substantial heterogeneity using the Chi-squared (Q2) and I squared tests, respectively. Forest plots were generated for each predefined outcome. We identified significant heterogeneity as a Breslow–Day test I 2 > 50% or a P value < 0.1. In the presence of significant heterogeneity, the random effect model was employed. The results of our NMA, including all estimated values, were presented in a league table for ease of comparison. Results Study Selection After removing duplicate entries, the initial electronic database searches yielded 377 unique records. Through the process of titles and abstracts screening, 285 were excluded. A total of 92 records for full text screening. Among these, 73 records were excluded owing to inappropriate study design, population, intervention, or lack of relevant outcomes. Among the remaining 19 studies [ – , – ], 2 studies compared [ , ] different routes for the same treatment, which are not relevant for the other study that does not mention the route of each drug or our network (Fig. ) Study Characteristics The objective of this clinical research paper was to assess the efficacy of different pulmonary vasodilators in patients undergoing mitral valve surgery. 17 studies [ , , – ] involving 862 patients were analyzed to investigate the impact of these vasodilators. The studies utilized various measurements to evaluate the outcomes. Those measurements were divided into three categories: pulmonary measures, systemic measures, and cardiac measures. In terms of pulmonary measures, four specific parameters were examined, mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP), systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (SPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCW). While systemic measures included three parameters, central venous pressure (CVP), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and mean arterial pressure (MAP). Cardiac measures included three parameters as well, cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (C.I), and heart rate (HR). The study examined ten unique treatment options, which were categorized into three groups. Group 1 included nitric oxide (NO), sodium nitroprusside, and nitroglycerin. Group 2 included phosphodiesterase inhibitors, such as enoximone and milrinone. Lastly, group 3 included prostacyclin analogues (prostacyclin and iloprost). The detailed summary and baseline characteristics for the included studies are presented in Tables and , respectively. Quality Assessment After applying The Cochrane Risk of Bias (ROB 2) tool to evaluate the quality of the included studies, most of the included studies showed low risk of bias in most of the domains. Ersoy 2013, Fattouch 2005, and Fattoucha 2006 [ , , ] showed high risk of bias owing to randomization, while Fattouch 2005 and Mishra 2016 [ , ] showed high risk of bias owing to missing data. Jiang 2013 and Eskandr 2018 [ , ] showed high risk of bias as well owing to selection of reported results. The rest of the studies showed low risk of overall bias. The risk of bias summary and graph are shown in Figs. and , respectively. Network Meta-Analysis Results We included 17 studies in the analysis. All the included studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that examined the effects of different vasodilators. The studies focused on three pulmonary measures, namely MPAP, SPAP, and PCWP, with 22, 8, and 15 pairwise comparisons, respectively. Systemic measures, including MAP and SVR, had 19 and 14 pairwise comparisons, while cardiac measures, such as HR and CI, had 13 and 19 pairwise comparisons. Although additional outcomes, such as PVR, CVP, and CO, were considered, no network meta-analyses (NMAs) could be performed owing to a lack of connectivity between treatments. Fixed-effects models were employed for all the measure except for MPAP, for which random-effects models were found to be more suitable for these two measures. The new model yielded no indicators of inconsistency, suggesting that the data included in the analysis were comparable. Pulmonary Measures Our analysis shows that none of the treatments showed significant efficacy compared to placebo in reducing PCWP and SPAP (Figs. , ). However, for MPAP, prostacyclin, nitric oxide (NO), and sodium nitroprusside demonstrated statistically significant reduction in MPAP when compared with placebo [MD, 95% CI: (− 11.77, − 18.78; − 4.76; − 8.3–15.9,−0.61; and − 11.02, − 20.1; − 3.8, respectively] (Fig. ). The heterogeneity was significant for MPAP and PCWP, ( I 2 = 61.6%, 26%, 80.1% and I 2 = 75%, 43.4%, 89%, respectively) indicating variability among the studies, while SPAP showed low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 22.7%, 0%, 73.4%). To address the heterogeneity and inconsistency, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by excluding the studies that contributed large heterogeneity and inconsistency for MAPAP and PCWP measures. Study 5 and 6 [ ] was excluded for MPAP, while studies 4 and 17 [ , ] were excluded for PCWP. The revised models showed improvements in model fit. Sildenafil showed a statistically significant reduction in MPAP (MD, 95% CI: (− 2.9, − 5.5; − 0.29), while both NO and sildenafil showed a statistically significant reduction in PCWP (MD, 95% CI: −6.64, −12.48; −0.80; 4.80, 0.90; 8.7) respectively. The heterogeneity in the revised models was reduced compared with the initial models ( I 2 = 46.1%,0%, 75% and I 2 = 28.3%, 0%, 73.4%). The observed heterogeneity for MPAP and PCWP was found to be specific to certain treatment comparisons rather than common across all comparisons. After conducting sensitivity analyses and excluding studies contributing to large heterogeneity (study 5 and 6 for MPAP and studies 4 and 17 for PCWP), the heterogeneity was reduced, indicating that the variability was driven primarily by these specific comparisons rather than being a generalized issue across all comparisons. We applied the SUCRA scores to rank the treatments based on their efficacy. Sildenafil (79%), nitric oxide(78%), and milrinone (89%) were ranked higher for decreasing MPAP, PCWP, and SPAP, respectively. Systemic Measures The analysis revealed that NO, prostacyclin, and sodium nitroprusside showed significant reductions in MAP, with effect sizes (MD, 95% CI: 24, 15; 33; 18.9, 10; 27.8; 22.6, 10; 27.8 , respectively) (Fig. ). Additionally, NO, prostacyclin, sodium nitroprusside, and nitroglycerin demonstrated significant reductions in systemic vascular resistance (SVR), with effect sizes of (MD, 95% CI: − 0.54, − 0.82; − 0.26; − 0.37, − 0.65; − 0.09; − 0.47, − 0.77; − 0.16; − 0.14, − 0.24; − 0.03, respectively) (Fig. ). The heterogeneity observed in the two models was low, with I 2 values of 0%. This indicates that there was a minimal variability among the studies included in the analysis. Furthermore, there was no evidence of inconsistency in either model, as indicated by the non-significant Q values ( I 2 = 0%, 0% ,67.6%; I 2 = 0%, 0%, 84.7%). Enoxamine was found to be the most effective in reducing MAP, with a SUCRA score of 81%. In contrast, NO had the lowest SUCRA score of 6%, suggesting it was the least effective in reducing MAP. For SVR, levosimendan had the highest positive impact with a SUCRA score of 91%, while sildenafil was the least likely to have a positive impact on SVR, with a SUCRA score of 12%. Cardiac Measures The analysis showed that none of the treatments had a significant effect on heart rate (HR) (Fig. ). However, several treatment options, including iloprost, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, nitric oxide (NO), and prostacyclin, showed significant increases in cardiac index (C.I). However, several treatment options, including iloprost, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, nitric oxide (NO), and prostacyclin, showed significant increases in cardiac index (C.I). The effect sizes for C.I were (MD, 95% CI: 0.98, 0.3; 1.7; 2.8, 1.8; 3.9; 3, 1.7; 4.3; 1, 0.3; 1.7; 1.2, 0.8; 1.6; 1.2, 0.8; 1.6, respectively) (Fig. ). The heterogeneity in both models was low, with I 2 values of 0%. ( I 2 = 0%, 0%, 67.6%; I 2 = 0%, 0%, 79.2%, respectively). Loprost was found to be the least effective in reducing heart rate with the lowest SUCRA score of 12%. For cardiac index, milrinone and levosimendan had the highest positive impact, with SUCRA scores of 95% and 92%, respectively. On the other hand, sildenafil was the least likely to have a positive impact on cardiac index, with a SUCRA score of 8%. Subgroup Analysis Regarding subgrouping, we split patients into those with heart failure and those without. For patients with heart failure, we looked at MPAP, PCWP, C.I, and HR using NMA. For patients without heart failure, we only considered SPAP. We could not perform NMA for the resting measure owing to a lack of connection between the designs. Patients with Heart Failure In patients with heart failure, NO showed a significant decrease in MPAP from the baseline (MD, 95% CI: 13.73, − 23.7; − 3.8 ), with a highest SUCRA score of 71%. I 2 for heterogeneity/inconsistency = 59.1% (0%, 84.7%) (Supp Fig.1). For PCWP, sildenafil exhibited a significant increase (MD, 95% CI: 4.8, 2.4; 7.3). NO ranked highest in terms of SUCRA score by 80% and a I 2 for heterogeneity/inconsistency = 48.1% (0%, 84.8%) (Supp Fig.2). In terms of cardiac index, sildenafil achieved the highest score of 96%, while levosimendan achieved the highest score for heart rate at 69%. I 2 for heterogeneity / inconsistency = 24.2% (0%, 92.1%) and 7% (0%, 90.3%), respectively (Supp Figs. 3 and 4). Patients Without Heart Failure Sildenafil shows significant reduction from the baseline for SPAP (MD, 95% CI: − 6.5, 12.3; − 0.83) and ranked highest in terms of SUCRA score at 86%. I 2 for heterogeneity/inconsistency = 0% (0%, 7%) (Supp Fig.5). Discussion Preoperative PH is a known risk factor for increased morbidity and mortality after mitral valve surgery [ ]. In this current network meta-analysis, the investigators compared the effect of various vasodilators in perioperative management of PH during mitral valve surgery. The primary findings showed the following: (I) prostacyclin, NO, and sodium nitroprusside demonstrated a significant reduction in MPAP; (II) none of the vasodilators showed significant efficacy in reducing PCWP or SPAP; (III) NO, prostacyclin, and sodium nitroprusside exhibited a significant reduction in MAP and SVR; (IV) enoximone showed the most reduction in MAP; (V) levosimendan had the highest positive impact on SVR; (VI) iloprost, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, NO, and prostacyclin showed a significant increase in the cardiac index (C.I), and the highest positive impact was with milrinone and levosimendan; (VII) none of the treatment options had a significant effect on HR; and (VIII) in patients with heart failure, NO significantly reduced MPAP, while sildenafil increased pressure PCWP and achieved the highest C.I. In patients without heart failure, sildenafil significantly reduced SPAP. The findings of our NMA offer a comprehensive understanding of the impact on cardiac performance. In a study by Patel et al., showed that several pulmonary vasodilators can be used in PH including inhaled prostacyclin and NO to reduce PAPs, PVR, and improve cardiac output in patients with pulmonary hypertension resulting from MVD after surgery. Though short‐term use of these pulmonary vasodilators in the postoperative period appears safe [ ]. Another study by Sardo et al., showed that inhaled prostacyclin was the only vasodilator whose use is supported by a statistically discernible improvement in mortality in the perioperative cardiac surgery setting as treatment of pulmonary hypertension [ ]. The clinical implications of these hemodynamic improvements, particularly their potential to translate into better postoperative outcomes, such as decreased morbidity, mortality, and long-term survival, need further clarification. While previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of reducing MPAP and improving C.I in the perioperative period [ , ], the mechanisms through which these improvements lead to better clinical outcomes, such as reduced right ventricular failure [ ], improved long-term cardiac function, and survival rates [ ], remain underexplored. For instance, PHTN is strongly associated with increased mortality and heart failure readmissions after mitral valve repair [ ], and postoperative hemodynamic factors, such as increased PAP and PVR, have been linked to worse outcomes, including right heart failure and mortality [ ]. The improvement in MPAP and C.I does suggest a beneficial effect, but long-term follow-up studies and more detailed investigations into patient-centered outcomes are necessary to confirm whether these hemodynamic changes translate into improved postoperative

to better clinical outcomes, such as reduced right ventricular failure [ ], improved long-term cardiac function, and survival rates [ ], remain underexplored. For instance, PHTN is strongly associated with increased mortality and heart failure readmissions after mitral valve repair [ ], and postoperative hemodynamic factors, such as increased PAP and PVR, have been linked to worse outcomes, including right heart failure and mortality [ ]. The improvement in MPAP and C.I does suggest a beneficial effect, but long-term follow-up studies and more detailed investigations into patient-centered outcomes are necessary to confirm whether these hemodynamic changes translate into improved postoperative recovery and survival [ , ]. Moreover, although our study highlights the effectiveness of vasodilators in managing perioperative pulmonary hypertension [ ], the literature lacks comprehensive evaluations of how these interventions impact long-term survival, quality of life, and the risk of complications, such as right-sided heart failure, arrhythmias, and prolonged ICU stay post-surgery [ ]. In a study on severe heart failure patients undergoing mitral valve repair, elevated biomarkers such as high-sensitive troponin T and low mixed venous oxygen saturation were predictive of worse prognosis, including increased mortality [ ]. Therefore, future studies should aim to bridge this gap by conducting longitudinal analyses that focus on these outcomes in the context of mitral valve surgery and heart failure management. Efforts to improve earlier intervention, before the onset of severe PHTN, may further enhance patient outcomes [ ]. Our analysis emphasized the challenge of managing PH during mitral valve surgery, where the patients face elevated risks of complications and mortality. The study aimed to provide more clarity in the selection of vasodilator agents, addressing the scarcity of solid evidence and the current reliance on individual judgment and existing meta-analyses. Strengths The study utilized a rigorous systematic review and meta-analysis approach following PRISMA guidelines. The inclusion of a network meta-analysis allowed for a comprehensive comparison of multiple vasodilators, providing a nuanced understanding of their efficacy. The sensitivity analysis addressed heterogeneity and inconsistency and enhanced the robustness of the findings. Limitations The study limitations include the presence of high risk of bias in some included studies. Additionally, heterogeneity and inconsistency were observed in certain outcomes, leading to the exclusion of specific studies in the sensitivity analysis. Finally, the lack of relationship between treatments with some outcomes restricted the conduct of network meta-analyses. Not all the medications discussed, such as milrinone, are specific pulmonary vasodilators. While milrinone primarily functions as an inotrope for heart failure, its inclusion in our analysis was on the basis of its vasodilatory effects and role in overall hemodynamic optimization. This broad approach to medication selection may limit the direct applicability of our findings to pulmonary hypertension management alone. Future studies could benefit from focusing more narrowly on interventions specifically targeting pulmonary hypertension to refine therapeutic strategies. Lastly, the data were not sufficient to conduct a reliable subgroup analysis based on the heart failure status of the patients in all the outcomes. Recommendations for Future Studies Future studies should focus on conducting well-designed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with low risk of bias to strengthen the evidence base. Addressing the limitations observed in this analysis, such as heterogeneity and inconsistency, will contribute to more reliable and generalizable findings. Further studies are warranted to explore the long-term outcomes and adverse effects of vasodilator in the context of PH during cardiac surgery. Conclusions In summary, our NMA highlights prostacyclin, NO, and sodium nitroprusside as consistently effective in reducing MPAP during mitral valve surgery in the setting of PH. These medications exhibit positive impacts on systemic parameters, lowering MAP and SVR. Milrinone and levosimendan emerge as valuable choices, enhancing C.I without significantly affecting HR. These findings offer insights for clinicians, suggesting prostacyclin, NO, sodium nitroprusside, milrinone, and levosimendan as promising options for perioperative optimization of hemodynamics in patients with PH prior to mitral valve surgery. While acknowledging study limitations, these results contribute to refining treatment strategies and call for future well-designed trials to explore long-term outcomes and adverse effects associated with these interventions. documents.title: SCAI Clinical expert consensus statement on cardiogenic shock

chunks.content: What is cardiogenic shock? Cardiogenic shock (CS) is a clinical syndrome characterized by systemic tissue hypoperfusion due to inadequate cardiac output, resulting in a life-threatening condition. Although the conceptual description of CS identifies a well-recognized clinical scenario, there are no universally accepted diagnostic criteria. Indeed, the definition of CS varies across randomized clinical trials and position papers issued by scientific societies ( ). Why cardiogenic shock? Cardiogenic shock is associated with a mortality rate ranging from 30% to 60%, with deaths predominantly occurring within the first hours and during the first month (70–80%). Despite significant scientific advances, mortality remains unacceptably high. Data from the Cath-PCI registry demonstrate that CS-related mortality has not improved over time; moreover, in patients with ischaemic CS, mortality has further increased, highlighting a clear disconnect between scientific progress and actual clinical outcomes. These findings reflect the limitations observed to date: clinical trials attempting to identify effective treatments for CS have often yielded inconclusive results, largely because they enrolled heterogeneous patient populations. Consequently, recognizing and phenotyping the different forms of CS is essential to enable the implementation of targeted and effective therapeutic strategies. Timing of intervention Management of cardiogenic shock must be rapid and focused, aiming to promptly identify the patient’s phenotype in order to initiate effective and personalized treatment strategies. The concept of the ‘ golden hour’ is therefore central to CS management. To integrate clinical phenotyping with therapeutic decision-making, we propose the FAST protocol ( ). Phenotyping Clinical phenotyping Phenotyping of cardiogenic shock may be aetiological, clinical, haemodynamic, or emo-metabolic. The most historically established approach is clinical phenotyping, which identifies four patient subtypes: Cold and wet : patients with reduced cardiac output and elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), representing approximately two-thirds of patients with ischaemic CS. Cold and dry : the so-called euvolaemic cardiogenic shock. Warm and wet : including CS associated with inflammatory response and peripheral vasodilation, normotensive CS, and CS due to right ventricular (RV) dysfunction. Normotensive CS had already been observed in early trials; for example, 5.2% of patients enrolled in the SHOCK trial were normotensive. Warm and dry : patients with preserved cardiac output, resembling a vasodilatory shock phenotype. Haemodynamic–aetiological phenotyping Alongside clinical phenotyping, aetiological classification allows identification of distinct CS subtypes: ischaemic CS , de novo heart failure–related CS , acute decompensation of chronic heart failure (ADHF) , secondary CS , and mixed shock . Twenty to twenty-five years ago, CS was predominantly secondary to acute myocardial infarction (AMI), accounting for approximately 80% of all cases. In recent decades, however, the prevalence of ischaemic CS has declined in favour of CS related to heart failure. A recent analysis from the Critical Care Cardiology Trials Network (CCCTN), using the Shock Academy Research Consortium (SHARC) definition, reported that 27% of CS cases were of ischaemic origin, whereas 59% were related to heart failure (72% ADHF and 28% de novo ). Patients with de novo heart failure–related CS have fewer comorbidities but exhibit higher 30-day mortality compared with those with CS due to ADHF. Furthermore, CCCTN data show that patients with ADHF-related CS and ischaemic CS more frequently present with cardiac arrest at onset, whereas patients with CS overlapping with non-cardiogenic shock components—the so-called mixed shock —have a worse prognosis and more severe clinical presentations. Mixed shock represents a condition in which cardiogenic shock, where an increase in systemic vascular resistance would be expected to compensate for reduced cardiac output, is complicated by inappropriate systemic vasodilation. Mixed shock was introduced as a distinct phenotype by the American Heart Association in 2017 and later by SHARC in 2023. According to CCCTN data, approximately 20% of patients admitted to intensive care units for shock actually present with mixed shock. Moreover, mixed shock may complicate nearly 25% of cardiogenic shock cases after a mean of only 5 days, conferring significantly higher mortality compared with pure cardiogenic shock. Mixed shock therefore represents a clinical turning point characterized by a steeper mortality trajectory. In this setting, haemodynamic deterioration can no longer be explained solely by pump failure but requires timely recognition of the development of a systemic inflammatory response and progressive vasoplegia. Emo-metabolic phenotyping and new perspectives In addition to the aetiological classification of CS, more recent models have been proposed that integrate haemodynamic assessment with metabolic profiling, some of which have been derived using machine learning (ML) analyses. Among the most relevant is the model proposed by Zweck et al. , which analysed patients with CS from international cohorts and identified three distinct CS phenotypes: non-congested , cardio-renal , and cardio-metabolic . The non-congested phenotype is characterized by lower central venous pressure (CVP) and higher arterial blood pressure. models have been proposed that integrate haemodynamic assessment with metabolic profiling, some of which have been derived using machine learning (ML) analyses. Among the most relevant is the model proposed by Zweck et al. , which analysed patients with CS from international cohorts and identified three distinct CS phenotypes: non-congested , cardio-renal , and cardio-metabolic . The non-congested phenotype is characterized by lower central venous pressure (CVP) and higher arterial blood pressure. The cardio-renal phenotype includes a higher prevalence of elderly, multi-morbid patients with worse renal function, reflected by elevated serum creatinine levels. The cardio-metabolic phenotype is characterized by higher arterial lactate levels, signs of multi-organ involvement, and increased CVP due to RV involvement. The three phenotypes showed progressively higher mortality rates of 21%, 45%, and 55%, respectively. Notably, despite these marked differences in mortality, patients across the three groups were treated in a similar manner, underscoring the lack of phenotype-guided therapeutic strategies. A second Italian study applied ML techniques to a cohort of patients with CS and identified five phenotypes: phenotype I, non-dilated left ventricle (LV) ; phenotype II, dilated LV ; phenotype III, RV dysfunction ; phenotype IV, advanced age with mild ventricular dysfunction ; and phenotype V, hypotension with severe renal failure . Phenotype classification was readily achievable through bedside clinical and echocardiographic assessment and was associated with progressively increasing mortality (hazard ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.07–1.57). These findings further confirm that patients with cardiogenic shock are not a homogeneous population and that accurate phenotyping enables more precise prognostic stratification and the potential for truly personalized, phenotype-guided therapy. Severity classification Once the patient’s phenotype has been identified, assessment of disease severity is essential. In this context, the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) classification , summarized in , has become widely adopted in daily clinical practice. The SCAI classification not only stratifies patient prognosis—with mortality increasing in parallel with worsening SCAI stage—but also serves as a dynamic tool for monitoring disease trajectory and should be reassessed whenever the patient’s clinical condition changes. Data from the Cardiogenic Shock Working Group (CSWG) registry demonstrate that patients initially classified as stage D who progress to stage E experience an in-hospital mortality of 53%, while patients initially in stage B who deteriorate to stage E reach mortality rates as high as 75%. Furthermore, according to CSWG data, approximately 90% of patients initially in stage B progress to a more advanced stage within the first 52 h, highlighting the critical importance of timely and repeated reassessment. These findings also emphasize that patients in SCAI stage B should not be underestimated. Invasive and non-invasive haemodynamic monitoring Invasive haemodynamic monitoring is performed using the Swan–Ganz (SG) pulmonary artery catheter . In the Evaluation Study of Congestive Heart Failure and Pulmonary Artery Catheterization Effectiveness (ESCAPE) trial, the use of the SG catheter did not demonstrate an improvement in event-free survival (Binanay et al. , 2005). However, retrospective registry data have shown that SG-guided monitoring is associated with reduced mortality in cardiogenic shock, particularly in patients with AMI and those receiving mechanical circulatory support. Non-invasive monitoring using echocardiography allows estimation of multiple haemodynamic parameters, including cardiac output (CO), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), pulmonary artery pulsatility index (PAPi), pulmonary and systemic vascular resistances, CVP, and cardiac power. A prospective Italian study demonstrated good agreement between invasive and non-invasive haemodynamic assessments for CVP, CO, and pulmonary artery pressure (correlation coefficient R > 0.8), with a more modest correlation for PAPi ( R = 0.67). Furthermore, analysis of the left ventricular pressure–volume (P–V) relationship throughout the cardiac cycle allows derivation of two parameters used to assess ventriculo–arterial coupling (VAC) : end-systolic elastance (Ees), a surrogate of left ventricular contractility, and arterial elastance (Ea), a surrogate of arterial load. Even without invasive reconstruction of the P–V loop, echocardiography enables estimation of the Ees/Ea ratio. A ratio close to 1 reflects a condition of maximal cardiac efficiency. Conversely, if a patient exhibits VAC < 1 due to low peripheral resistance (Ea < 2) with preserved Ees, vasopressor therapy is likely to be beneficial. If, instead, VAC > 1 is driven by elevated Ea, the patient may benefit from inodilator therapy. Ventriculo–arterial coupling can also be assessed for the right ventricle (RV) using PAPi as a surrogate of RV Ees. A normal PAPi associated with low pulmonary Ea indicates a physiological state; a reduced PAPi in the presence of low pulmonary Ea suggests isolated RV dysfunction; and a reduced PAPi combined with elevated pulmonary Ea indicates biventricular dysfunction with an unfavourable prognosis. A normal PAPi associated with low pulmonary Ea indicates a physiological state; a reduced PAPi in the presence of low pulmonary Ea suggests isolated RV dysfunction; and a reduced PAPi combined with elevated pulmonary Ea indicates biventricular dysfunction with an unfavourable prognosis. Treatment Pharmacological treatment Once the patient has been characterized according to phenotype and severity, treatment should be tailored accordingly. The mechanisms of action of the main pharmacological agents are summarized in . Epinephrine has been evaluated in several clinical trials, the most notable being the OPTIMA CC trial (Epinephrine Versus Norepinephrine for Cardiogenic Shock After Acute Myocardial Infarction), which was terminated prematurely due to a higher incidence of refractory shock in the epinephrine arm. With regard to dopamine, a subanalysis of the SOAP III trial in patients with cardiogenic shock reported an increase in heart rate and myocardial oxygen consumption. Among alternative drug classes, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, such as milrinone and enoximone, may be used. The DOREMI trial (Dobutamine Compared with Milrinone in the Treatment of Cardiogenic Shock) randomized patients with cardiogenic shock to dobutamine vs. milrinone and found no significant difference in the primary composite endpoint. Among calcium sensitizers, levosimendan deserves mention. Several studies have investigated levosimendan; in the LIDO study, patients with cardiogenic shock due to acute decompensated heart failure were randomized to levosimendan or dobutamine, with levosimendan proving more effective in achieving the primary haemodynamic endpoint of increased cardiac output. Owing to its long-acting metabolite, levosimendan has also been shown to reduce hospitalizations in patients with advanced heart failure treated with intermittent infusions, as demonstrated in the LION-HEART trial. Among less frequently used agents, vasopressin may be beneficial in mixed shock or in cases of refractory hypotension associated with right ventricular dysfunction, as its vasoconstrictive effects spare the pulmonary circulation. Finally, methylene blue merits consideration in selected cases of mixed shock. However, the supporting evidence remains limited, and its use may be associated with serious adverse effects, including serotonin syndrome when administered concomitantly with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Mechanical circulatory support Mechanical circulatory support devices differ in their mechanism of action, vascular access requirements, and the degree of haemodynamic support provided. The intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) was evaluated in the IABP-SHOCK II trial, which assessed its use in patients with ischaemic cardiogenic shock and found no mortality benefit. However, the study had several limitations, including a high crossover rate between treatment arms and variable timing of device insertion, with 85% of placements occurring after percutaneous coronary intervention. More recently, the Altshock-2 trial (Study on Early Intra-aortic Balloon Pump Placement in Acute Decompensated Heart Failure Complicated by Cardiogenic Shock) randomized patients with cardiogenic shock due to heart failure to early IABP implantation vs. standard therapy, with the primary endpoint of 60-day survival or successful bridging to heart transplantation. The trial yielded neutral results. However, patients were highly selected and predominantly exhibited a low-output syndrome rather than overt cardiogenic shock, as reflected by relatively low mean arterial lactate levels (1.8 mmol/L). Indeed, 75% of patients in the non-IABP group survived to 60 days or were successfully transplanted. Escalating the level of mechanical support, Impella® is a percutaneous microaxial flow pump with an inlet positioned in the left ventricle and an outlet in the ascending aorta. Recently, the multicentre DanGer Shock trial (Microaxial Flow Pump or Standard Care in Infarct-Related Cardiogenic Shock) reported highly relevant results. This study randomized patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by CS—defined by laboratory evidence of peripheral hypoperfusion, hypotension, and left ventricular ejection fraction < 45%—to standard care alone or standard care plus implantation of an Impella CP device. The trial demonstrated a significant reduction in 180-day mortality of 13% in the Impella group. The study population was predominantly male (79%), with a mean age of 79 years, and patients were randomized early (mean time from symptom onset of 4 h). Approximately 84% of enrolments occurred in the cardiac catheterization laboratory. Most patients were classified as SCAI stage C (55%), with the remaining 45% in stages D or E. The mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 25%, and baseline arterial lactate levels averaged 4.5 mmol/L. Most infarctions were anterior or extensive anterior myocardial infarctions, with 74% involving the left main coronary artery or the left anterior descending artery as the culprit lesion. In addition to reduced mortality, subanalyses showed that Impella implantation in the DanGer Shock trial was associated with more rapid lactate clearance (approximately 12 h earlier than standard care), reduced requirements for inotropes and vasopressors, and improved mean arterial pressure. However, despite the favourable impact on the primary endpoint, the Impella group experienced a higher incidence of adverse events, including major bleeding, limb ischaemia, or haemolysis, occurring in 24% of cases compared with 6.2% in the standard-care group. However, despite the favourable impact on the primary endpoint, the Impella group experienced a higher incidence of adverse events, including major bleeding, limb ischaemia, or haemolysis, occurring in 24% of cases compared with 6.2% in the standard-care group. These findings suggest that the substantial benefit of mechanical circulatory support with Impella should be reserved for carefully selected patients, in order to maximize survival benefit while minimizing complications. Conclusions In summary, cardiogenic shock should not be considered a single, monolithic entity, but rather a complex and heterogeneous spectrum of clinical, aetiological, haemodynamic, and emo-metabolic phenotypes. The ability to accurately phenotype each patient is fundamental to selecting the most appropriate therapeutic strategy. Only through such stratification can advanced therapies be allocated to patients who are most likely to derive meaningful benefit, while simultaneously minimizing treatment-related risks.

documents.title: SCAI SHOCK stage classification expert consensus update

chunks.content: Introduction Cardiogenic shock (CS) is the most severe presentation of acute heart failure and is characterized by a critical reduction in cardiac output leading to systemic hypoperfusion, cellular dysoxia, and progressive multi-organ dysfunction [ ]. Despite advances in early revascularization, pharmacological therapy, and temporary mechanical circulatory support (t-MCS), mortality remains high, ranging from 30% to more than 50% in contemporary cohorts [ , , , ], making it one of the most lethal forms of circulatory shock [ , ]. Among the numerous clinical, hemodynamic, and biological markers used to assess severity and guide management, blood lactate concentration has emerged as one of the most robust and reproducible prognostic indicators in CS [ , , , , ]. Lactate measurement is part of the SHARC (Scientific Expert Panel From the Shock Academic Research Consortium) criteria for diagnosing CS, where a level >2 mmol/L serves as an optional marker of tissue hypoperfusion [ ]. The revised Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) staging system for CS integrates new lactate thresholds with Stages A and B characterized by normal lactate concentrations, Stages C and D >2 mmol/L, and Stage E >8 mmol/L [ ]. Furthermore, serial lactate monitoring is strongly endorsed by both the ACC Expert Consensus Statement Concise Clinical Guidance on CS [ ] and the most recent ESC guidelines for the management of CS [ ]. Traditionally regarded as a marker of anaerobic metabolism and tissue hypoxia, lactate is now recognized as a dynamic integrative signal reflecting the interaction between oxygen delivery, microcirculatory function, metabolic stress, adrenergic activation, and organ-specific clearance ( ) [ , , , ]. The classic historical classification proposed by Cohen and Woods in the 1980s divided lactic acidosis into two major entities: type A, resulting from impaired tissue perfusion or oxygen delivery, and type B, characterized by lactate accumulation in the absence of overt hypoxia, often linked to metabolic derangements or impaired clearance [ ]. Recently, building on this framework, Muller et al. introduced a mechanism-oriented classification that more precisely reflects the biological drivers of lactate elevation. This updated model delineates three dominant pathways [ ]: increased pyruvate generation due to nonspecific acceleration of glycolysis, such as that induced by catecholamine excess, β-agonists, respiratory alkalosis, or metabolic stress [ ]; reduced pyruvate utilization secondary to tissue hypoxia; and [ ] impaired lactate clearance, most commonly observed in the setting of advanced hepatic or renal dysfunction ( ) [ ]. However, in CS, these multiple mechanisms frequently coexist and overlap, substantially increasing the complexity of clinical interpretation. Beyond its prognostic value, lactate has gained increasing importance as a marker of treatment response and may even represent an adaptive metabolic substrate under conditions of cardiac stress [ , , ]. This evolving understanding challenges the long-standing perception of lactate as a mere by-product of shock [ ] and has important implications for clinical interpretation and therapeutic strategy [ , , ]. Pathophysiology of lactate in cardiogenic shock (<xref rid="fig0010" ref-type="fig">Fig. 2</xref>) Lactate production under aerobic and anaerobic conditions Lactate is continuously produced through the conversion of pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase, even under aerobic conditions. Lactate production is primarily determined by glycolytic flux rather than oxygen availability per se [ , ]. Under resting conditions, the weight-adjusted daily production of lactate in humans is estimated to be 20 mmol/kg. Indeed, in a standard 70-kg adult, daily lactate production is approximately 1,400 mmol, originating from the skeletal muscles (25%), skin (25%), brain (20%), erythrocytes (20%), and gastrointestinal tract (10%) [ ]. Thus, in physiological states, lactate serves as a central metabolic intermediate facilitating the transfer of carbon substrates and reducing equivalents between tissues, a concept formalized in the “lactate shuttle” theory [ , ]. In CS, hyperlactatemia reflects an imbalance between ongoing lactate production and its removal from the blood through excretion (e.g., urine, sweat) and metabolism (e.g., cellular uptake as a direct energy source, hepatic conversion to glucose), rather than a single mechanism. Impaired oxygen delivery, microcirculatory dysfunction, adrenergic stimulation, mitochondrial alterations, and reduced hepatic or renal clearance may all contribute simultaneously [ ]. Global hypoperfusion and anaerobic glycolysis The most intuitive mechanism of lactate elevation in CS is global hypoperfusion due to reduced cardiac output. When systemic oxygen delivery (DO₂) falls below a critical threshold, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation becomes insufficient to meet cellular energy demands, leading to a shift toward anaerobic glycolysis. Under these hypoxic conditions, glycolysis of glucose generates pyruvate, which is then preferentially converted into lactate (reduction by L-lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)), allowing regeneration of NAD + and continuation of glycolysis [ ]. This mechanism predominates in the early and most severe phases of CS and is typically associated with other markers of global hypoxia, such as low mixed venous oxygen saturation and metabolic acidosis [ ]. Normal lactate/pyruvate (LP) ratio is around 10. An

systemic oxygen delivery (DO₂) falls below a critical threshold, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation becomes insufficient to meet cellular energy demands, leading to a shift toward anaerobic glycolysis. Under these hypoxic conditions, glycolysis of glucose generates pyruvate, which is then preferentially converted into lactate (reduction by L-lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)), allowing regeneration of NAD + and continuation of glycolysis [ ]. This mechanism predominates in the early and most severe phases of CS and is typically associated with other markers of global hypoxia, such as low mixed venous oxygen saturation and metabolic acidosis [ ]. Normal lactate/pyruvate (LP) ratio is around 10. An elevated lactate/pyruvate ratio suggests a decrease in cytoplasmic redox state toward increased NADH/NAD + , usually reflecting tissue hypoxia. In CS, Levy et al. found a value of 40+/-6 [ ]. Consistent with this concept, Rimachi et al. demonstrated in CS patients that serial measurements of lactate and pyruvate revealed an increased lactate/pyruvate ratio during the early hypoperfusion phase, supporting the hypothesis that anaerobic metabolism is the primary driver of hyperlactatemia in the early stages of shock [ ]. Moreover, Revelly et al., using infused ¹³C-labeled lactate (a stable, non-radioactive isotope tracer enabling quantification of lactate kinetics), demonstrated that in CS, hyperlactatemia is primarily driven by increased endogenous lactate production, whereas metabolic clearance appears comparatively less affected [ ]. Microcirculatory dysfunction and loss of hemodynamic coherence Beyond macrocirculatory failure, and similarly to other types of shock, severe or persistent CS may induce profound microcirculatory alterations, including reduced functional capillary density, heterogeneous blood flow distribution, and impaired oxygen extraction [ ]. These abnormalities may persist despite normalization of macrohemodynamic variables such as systemic blood pressure or cardiac output, leading to a loss of hemodynamic coherence between macro and microcirculation [ ]. As a result, regional hypoxia and lactate production may occur even when global DO₂ appears adequate, explaining persistent hyperlactatemia despite apparent hemodynamic stabilization [ ]. Indirect assessment of tissue perfusion can be performed using several bedside markers that correlate with lactate levels in early shock, such as urine output (though its interpretation is limited by the frequent use of diuretics for congestion management and the high prevalence of type 1 acute cardiorenal syndrome in CS), capillary refill time (CRT) [ ], mottling score [ , ], and the venous-to-arterial CO₂ gap [ ]. Interestingly, in a study by Merdji et al., CRT and skin mottling, two well-established clinical markers of microcirculatory dysfunction [ , ], were more strongly correlated with lactate levels than traditional macrocirculatory parameters, such as blood pressure or cardiac output in CS [ ]. Similar to lactate, these readily available and cost-free bedside markers have demonstrated strong prognostic relevance in early CS [ , ], although their interpretation has recognized limitations [ ]. Adrenergic-driven aerobic glycolysis CS is associated with intense endogenous catecholamine release and often requires administration of exogenous vasoactive agents. β-adrenergic stimulation increases glycolytic flux via activation of key enzymes and Na + /K + -ATPase activity, leading to increased lactate production even in the presence of sufficient oxygen availability [ , ]. This phenomenon, often referred to as aerobic glycolysis or stress hyperlactatemia, is particularly relevant in patients receiving epinephrine and may result in lactate elevation independent of tissue hypoxia, complicating clinical interpretation. Consistent with this mechanism, the OPTIMA-CC trial reported that epinephrine (a powerful β-adrenergic agonist) administration in acute myocardial infarction (AMI)–related CS was associated not only with higher heart rates and a greater risk of refractory CS, but also with substantially higher lactate concentrations, approximately twofold greater than those observed with norepinephrine or dobutamine, reinforcing the role of catecholamine-driven aerobic glycolysis [ ]. In line with these findings, the study by Léopold et al. [ ] also demonstrated potentially deleterious effects of epinephrine compared with norepinephrine in CS. Taken together, these data suggest that epinephrine should be avoided whenever possible in CS. Conversely, in patients with acute-on-chronic heart failure–related CS receiving long-term non-selective β-blocker therapy, lactate levels at shock onset may be artificially attenuated, potentially leading to underestimation of shock severity when relying on lactate alone. Supporting this observation, prior studies have shown that patients on chronic or premorbid β-blocker therapy are less likely to develop marked hyperlactatemia (≥4 mmol/L) during sepsis or septic shock and exhibit lower initial lactate concentrations compared with patients not receiving β-blockers [ , ]. A similar pattern is observed in β-blocker poisoning, in which early lactate elevation often seems disproportionately low relative to the clinical severity of CS [ ]. This effect likely reflects attenuation of β₂-adrenergic–mediated aerobic glycolysis and reduced lactate generation [ ]. However, although significantly lower lactate levels have been reported in some studies among patients with acute-on-chronic heart failure (HF)-CS compared with those with de-novo HF–CS [ ], this difference is not consistently observed across studies [ , ]. One potential explanation

A similar pattern is observed in β-blocker poisoning, in which early lactate elevation often seems disproportionately low relative to the clinical severity of CS [ ]. This effect likely reflects attenuation of β₂-adrenergic–mediated aerobic glycolysis and reduced lactate generation [ ]. However, although significantly lower lactate levels have been reported in some studies among patients with acute-on-chronic heart failure (HF)-CS compared with those with de-novo HF–CS [ ], this difference is not consistently observed across studies [ , ]. One potential explanation is that most patients with chronic heart failure are currently treated with cardioselective β-blockers rather than non-selective agents, which may differentially influence lactate production [ ]. Impaired lactate clearance Lactate clearance is primarily mediated by the liver (60%) via gluconeogenesis and oxidation, with additional contributions from the kidneys (30%) through similar mechanisms, with urinary excretion serving only a minor role in clearance (<10%) [ ] and other organs. In an ancillary analysis of the CardShock study, patients with abnormal liver function tests consistent with hypoxic hepatitis (defined by an ALT increase >20%) exhibited significantly higher lactate levels in CS, which remained elevated throughout the first 24 h compared with patients without hypoxic hepatitis [ ]. Hepatic lactate uptake is highly flow-dependent and requires adequate oxygenation. In CS, hepatic hypoperfusion, venous congestion, ischemic hepatitis, and acute kidney injury frequently impair lactate clearance, contributing to persistent hyperlactatemia even after partial restoration of perfusion [ , , , ]. Interestingly, existing evidence indicates that hemofiltration during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) has only a negligible impact on lactate clearance [ , ]. Lactate as a key oxidative fuel for the heart during systemic stress The heart has an exceptionally high and continuous energy demand, requiring sustained production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to preserve contractile function, with an estimated consumption of approximately 1 mmol of ATP per second. In the absence of ongoing ATP resynthesis, myocardial ATP stores would be exhausted within 2–10 seconds, resulting in rapid contractile failure. Continuous ATP generation is therefore indispensable for maintaining normal cardiac performance [ ]. Myocardial energy production relies almost exclusively on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, which depends on oxygen utilization within mitochondria and accounts for more than 90% of total ATP generation. This reliance underlies the remarkably high myocardial oxygen extraction, such that venous blood draining from the coronary sinus exhibits an oxygen saturation of ≈40%, representing the most deoxygenated venous blood in the body [ ]. This substantial energetic demand is met through metabolic flexibility, allowing the myocardium (a “metabolic omnivore”) to oxidize a range of substrates including fatty acids, glucose, ketone bodies, and lactate to sustain ATP production via mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (re 2 and 3) [ ]. Once generated, approximately 60%–70% of myocardial ATP is devoted to mechanical contraction, while the remaining 30%–40% supports ionic homeostasis, predominantly through ATP-dependent ion transport processes, particularly sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca² + -ATPase–mediated calcium handling [ ]. In this context, lactate should not be regarded solely as a marker of metabolic failure. Experimental and physiological studies demonstrate that lactate is a preferred oxidative substrate for the stressed myocardium and can support ATP generation when fatty acid and glucose metabolism are impaired [ , , ]. In a healthy porcine model, sodium lactate infusion has been reported to increase cardiac output, accompanied by a concurrent rise in whole-body oxygen consumption, consistent with oxidative metabolism of lactate [ ]. In a porcine model of ischemic CS, lactate infusion has been shown to improve cardiac output, stroke volume, and myocardial mechanical efficiency, while enhancing mitochondrial respiration, particularly when combined with inotropic stimulation [ , ]. In a rodent model of septic shock, Levy et al. demonstrated that systemic lactate deprivation adversely affected myocardial energetics, cardiovascular performance, and survival, underscoring lactate’s role as a critical metabolic substrate [ ]. Consistent findings have also been reported in rodent models of hemorrhagic shock, in which lactate supplementation improved hemodynamic and metabolic outcomes [ ]. In humans, lactate has similarly demonstrated cardiometabolic benefits [ ]. In healthy volunteers, infusion of half-molar sodium lactate enhanced cardiac performance, as evidenced by increases in cardiac output, stroke volume, and left ventricular ejection fraction, compared with sodium-matched hypertonic saline, suggesting a direct energetic and functional advantage beyond osmotic or volume effects [ ]. In patients with acute heart failure, infusion of half-molar sodium lactate has been shown to increase cardiac output and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) compared with control treatment [ ]. Similar benefits have been reported in patients after coronary artery bypass grafting, in whom lactate infusion significantly increased cardiac index relative to control [ ]. These data suggest that lactate can serve as a preferential oxidative substrate under stress conditions. However, whether systemic hyperlactatemia in CS

In patients with acute heart failure, infusion of half-molar sodium lactate has been shown to increase cardiac output and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) compared with control treatment [ ]. Similar benefits have been reported in patients after coronary artery bypass grafting, in whom lactate infusion significantly increased cardiac index relative to control [ ]. These data suggest that lactate can serve as a preferential oxidative substrate under stress conditions. However, whether systemic hyperlactatemia in CS represents a protective adaptive response or merely reflects metabolic stress occurring in parallel with substrate utilization remains uncertain. The presence of lactate-consuming organs does not imply that its systemic elevation is intrinsically beneficial ( ). Therefore, although experimental and preliminary clinical data suggest potential metabolic benefits of lactate infusion, evidence remains insufficient to support routine therapeutic use in CS. Prognostic Value of Lactate in Cardiogenic Shock Baseline lactate Admission lactate has long been associated with mortality in CS. Thresholds around 3.0–3.5 mmol/L consistently identify patients at high risk of short-term death [ , , ]. In one of the largest studies evaluating the prognostic value of lactate levels in AMI-CS, the optimal baseline lactate cutoff for predicting 30-day mortality was 5.0 mmol/L [ ]. However, baseline lactate is influenced by pre-hospital delay, early resuscitation, and catecholamine exposure, limiting its ability to discriminate reversibility once treatment has begun. It should be noted that arterial and central venous lactate concentrations are generally closely correlated in shock states; however, regional gradients may exist in the presence of severe splanchnic ischemia or impaired hepatic clearance. In clinical practice, serial measurements from the same sampling site are preferable to avoid misinterpretation of trends. In cardiac intensive care patients with a high inotrope/vasopressor score, Vanderbriele et al. founded a close correlation between radial and mixed venous lactate (from pulmonary artery catheter) [ ]. Nevertheless, it should be emphasized that these findings cannot be extrapolated to peripheral venous lactate, which may be influenced by local tissue metabolism, perfusion gradients, and regional metabolic activity. Indeed, several studies have reported that the difference between peripheral venous and arterial lactate measurements can be substantial, with venous values ranging from more than 3.5 mmol/L higher to 2.3 mmol/L lower than arterial levels. Such wide variability highlights the potential for clinically misleading interpretations when these sampling sites are used interchangeably [ ]. Dynamic lactate monitoring Serial lactate measurements provide superior prognostic information compared with isolated values [ , , , ]. Persistent hyperlactatemia or rising lactate trajectories identify patients with refractory shock, ongoing microcirculatory dysfunction, or impaired metabolic recovery, even when macrocirculatory targets appear achieved. In a substudy of the IABP-SHOCK II trial and its associated registry, investigators evaluated the prognostic value of arterial lactate at baseline, 8-h lactate, and early lactate clearance for predicting 30-day mortality in patients with AMI–related CS. Lactate measured at 8 h demonstrated superior prognostic accuracy compared with both baseline lactate and lactate clearance. Among all lactate-derived metrics, an 8-h lactate threshold of 3.1 mmol/L after initial management provided the best discriminatory performance for early risk stratification in CS [ ]. Lactate reduction and lactate load A reduction in lactate levels during the first 12–24 h has consistently been associated with improved survival in CS. Lactate appears to provide its strongest prognostic signal during the early phase of CS [ ], with its predictive accuracy declining beyond the first 24 h [ ]. However, focusing solely on the rate of lactate decline may underestimate the prognostic burden of sustained hyperlactatemia. To address this limitation, the concept of “normalized lactate load”, which integrates both the magnitude and duration of lactate elevation, has demonstrated superior prognostic performance in critically ill patients and in CS cohorts [ , ]. In a post hoc analysis of the DOREMI trial (Dobutamine Compared to Milrinone in the Treatment of Cardiogenic Shock), complete lactate clearance emerged as the strongest predictor of survival across all evaluated time points. The prognostic impact increased over time, with odds ratios for survival increasing from ≈2.5 at 8 h to ≈5.5 at 24 h [ ]. Lactate in risk stratification scores Lactate has been incorporated into most validated CS risk scores. In the CardShock score, lactate ≥2 mmol/L was independently associated with 30-day mortality [ ]. In the CLIP (cystatin C, lactate, IL-6, and NT-proBNP) score, lactate carries one of the highest normalized coefficients, indicating a major contribution to 30-day mortality prediction. Notably, during the development of this score, lactate was identified as one of the four most robust predictors from an initial pool of 58 candidate biomarkers [ ]. Similarly, in the Cardiogenic Shock Score, lactate ≥4 mmol/L identifies patients at markedly higher risk of short-term mortality [

stratification scores Lactate has been incorporated into most validated CS risk scores. In the CardShock score, lactate ≥2 mmol/L was independently associated with 30-day mortality [ ]. In the CLIP (cystatin C, lactate, IL-6, and NT-proBNP) score, lactate carries one of the highest normalized coefficients, indicating a major contribution to 30-day mortality prediction. Notably, during the development of this score, lactate was identified as one of the four most robust predictors from an initial pool of 58 candidate biomarkers [ ]. Similarly, in the Cardiogenic Shock Score, lactate ≥4 mmol/L identifies patients at markedly higher risk of short-term mortality [ ]. In patients receiving VA-ECMO, both the ENCOURAGE and SAVE scores include lactate as a major determinant of outcome [ , ]. Across all models, lactate consistently remains one of the strongest predictors of mortality. Based on these data, and drawing on the framework proposed by Naidu et al., we propose a bedside diagnostic algorithm that integrates lactate kinetics with peripheral perfusion markers in CS ( ) [ ]. Lactate and mechanical circulatory support CS patients supported with venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) present unique challenges. They commonly experience substantial ischemic-reperfusion injuries, receive high doses of catecholamines, and frequently suffer from both liver and kidney dysfunction based on the severity and duration of low cardiac output syndrome. Additionally, approximately 50% of these patients have undergone cardiac arrest [ ]. Furthermore, the degree and reversibility of myocardial failure and complications associated with VA-ECMO may influence the relationship between lactate levels, changes in lactate, and time to lactate normalization, and early or late survival. Pre-VA-ECMO lactate levels have been linked to prognosis [ , ] or included in several prognostic scores [ , ]. A recent meta-analysis and systematic review have brought to light that a reduction in lactate levels is associated with improved prognoses in CS, which includes a subgroup of patients supported by VA-ECMO [ ]. In a post hoc analysis of the HYPO-ECMO study, Levy et al. found [ ] a consistent and significant association between lactate levels, whether assessed at baseline or during ICU treatment, and the risk of mortality, which underscores the pivotal prognostic relevance of lactate levels in patients with CS undergoing VA-ECMO therapy. Beyond absolute lactate values, the study provided novel insights into lactate kinetics, demonstrating that the occurrence of a secondary lactate peak within the first 7 days after VA-ECMO initiation (observed in approximately 24% of patients) was independently associated with worse outcomes, regardless of baseline lactate levels. In a DanGer-SHOCK substudy, patients randomized to microaxial flow pump support exhibited faster lactate clearance and achieved complete normalization approximately 12 h earlier than those receiving standard care, despite comparable baseline lactate levels [ ]. Conclusion Lactate is a central integrative biomarker in CS, reflecting hypoperfusion, metabolic stress, adrenergic activation, and impaired clearance. Dynamic assessment of lactate kinetics rather than static values alone provides robust prognostic information and insight into shock reversibility. In the era of t-MCS, lactate remains both a guide and a potential therapeutic target, underscoring its pivotal role in the management of cardiogenic shock.
